title: حِكَايَةُ الْعَاشِقِ وَالْمَعْشُوقِ
titleEn: The Lover and the Beloved, continued
part: Night 111 · The Lover and the Beloved, continued
source: William Hay Macnaghten, ed., The Alif Laila, or Book of the Thousand Nights and One Night, vol. 1, Calcutta 1839 (“Calcutta II”), printed pp. 563–566 (Night 111, continuing directly from nights-110), transcribed from the 300 ppi scan (archive.org aliflailaorbooko01macn) by the editors' own transcription. The edition prints the prose essentially unpointed: ALL VOCALIZATION (tashkīl) IS EDITORIAL — ours, not the edition's — and the alphabet button strips it back to the bare rasm as Macnaghten prints it, except where a clear misprint has been corrected (each is noted). Romanization is simplified IJMES. Spelling, including the edition’s Middle Arabic forms, is preserved; clear misprints are corrected in the text, and the note on each gives the print’s reading. Obscure or doubtful forms are kept as printed, vocalized by evident sense and flagged in the notes. Read-aloud audio is a Modern Standard Arabic reading of this vocalised text, synthesized by machine, with word-by-word timing generated the same way.
about: Night 111 continues the story that the vizier Dandān tells within the tale of King ʿUmar ibn al-Nuʿmān, the story of the lover, the beloved and the go-between. Out hunting, Tāj al-Mulūk has noticed among a merchant caravan a handsome young man worn pale by grief, who recites a poem of parting, faints, and on coming to recites another on a woman’s murderous eyes. The prince goes to him, asks why he kept his goods back, and promises to right any wrong or pay any debt. Seated on a carpet before the prince’s ivory-and-ebony chair, the young man is made to unpack his bales; as he unfolds a gold-woven satin robe worth two thousand dinars, a scrap of cloth falls out of it, which he snatches up and hides under his thigh, reciting poems of longing as he goes. The prince asks to see it, and the young man answers that it was only for its sake that he would not show his goods. Five poems run through the night. As with every printed edition of the Nights, this one belongs to the late Egyptian recension (ZER) — an eighteenth-century expansion padded out to a literal 1001 nights; no printed edition is a medieval text, and Macnaghten regularised the language here and there, so some Middle Arabic texture is a nineteenth-century retrofit.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا كَانَتِ اللَّيْلَةُ الْحَادِيَةَ عَشَرَ بَعْدَ الْمِائَةِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā kānati al-laylatu al-ḥādiyata ʿashara baʿda al-miʾati
sentences.l: And when it was the night, the eleventh after the hundred,
sentences.i: And when it was the hundred and eleventh night,
sentences.n: al-ḥādiyata ʿashara, “eleventh”: the print has عشر where Classical Arabic would make the second part feminine (ʿashrata) to agree with the night; it is vocalised as printed. Compound numbers of this kind keep a fixed -a ending whatever their case.

sentences.t: قَالَتْ بَلَغَنِي أَيُّهَا الْمَلِكُ السَّعِيدُأَنَّ تَاجَ الْمُلُوكِ لَاحَتْ مِنْهُ الْتِفَاتَةٌ إِلَى الْقَافِلَةِ فَرَأَى شَابًّا جَمِيلَ الشَّبَابِ نَظِيفَ الثِّيَابِ ظَرِيفَ الْمَعَانِي إِلَّا أَنَّ ذَلِكَ الشَّابَّ قَدْ تَغَيَّرَتْ مَحَاسِنُهُ وَعَلَاهُ الِاصْفِرَارُ مِنْ فُرْقَةِ الْأَحْبَابِ وَزَادَهُ الْأَنِينُ وَالِانْتِحَابُ وَسَالَتْ مِنْ جَفْنَيْهِ الْعَبَرَاتُ وَهُوَ يُنْشِدُ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: qālat balaghanī ayyuhā al-maliku al-saʿīdu anna tāja al-mulūki lāḥat minhu iltifātatun ilā al-qāfilati fa-raʾā shābban jamīla al-shabābi naẓīfa al-thiyābi ẓarīfa al-maʿānī illā anna dhālika al-shābba qad taghayyarat maḥāsinuhu wa-ʿalāhu al-iṣfirāru min furqati al-aḥbābi wa-zādahu al-anīnu wa-al-intiḥābu wa-sālat min jafnayhi al-ʿabarātu wa-huwa yunshidu hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: She said: It has reached me, O king the happy, that Tāj al-Mulūk — there appeared from him a turning-glance toward the caravan, and he saw a youth, beautiful of youth, clean of clothes, elegant of qualities; except that that youth — his beauties had changed, and the yellowness had come-over him from the parting of the loved-ones, and the moaning and the sobbing had increased him, and there flowed from his two eyelids the tears, and he was reciting these verses:
sentences.i: She said: It has reached me, O fortunate king, that Tāj al-Mulūk happened to glance back at the caravan and saw a young man in the full beauty of youth, neatly dressed and graceful in manner; but that young man’s good looks had faded, and the pallor of parting from those he loved had come over him. He moaned and sobbed more and more, tears ran from his eyes, and he was reciting these verses:
sentences.n: Shahrazād takes up the night by repeating the end of the one before. The print runs al-saʿīd and anna together (السعيدان). zādahu al-anīnu wa-al-intiḥābu, literally “the moaning and sobbing increased him”: they grew on him. Rhymed prose: al-shabāb, al-thiyāb, al-aḥbāb, al-intiḥāb; then al-ʿabarāt, al-abyāt.

sentences.t:
طَالَ الْفِرَاقُ وَدَامَ الْهَمُّ وَالْوَجَلُ * وَالدَّمْعُ مِنْ مُقْلَتِي يَاصَاحِ مُنْهَمِلُ
وَالْعَتْبُ وَدَّعْتُهُ يَوْمَ الْفِرَاقِ وَقُلْ * بَقِيتُ فَرْدًا فَلَا قَلْبٌ وَلَا اَمَلُ
يَا صَاحِبِي قِفْ مَعِي حَتَّى اُوَدِّعَ مَنْ * مِنْ نُطْقِهَا تَشْتَفِى الْاَمْرَاضُ وَالْعِلَلُ
sentences.tr:
ṭāla al-firāqu wa-dāma al-hammu wa-al-wajalu * wa-al-damʿu min muqlatī yā ṣāḥi munhamilu
wa-al-ʿatbu waddaʿtuhu yawma al-firāqi wa-qul * baqītu fardan fa-lā qalbun wa-lā amalu
yā ṣāḥibī qif maʿī ḥattā uwaddiʿa man * min nuṭqihā tashtafī al-amrāḍu wa-al-ʿilalu
sentences.l:
Long-grew the parting, and lasted the care and the fear, and the tear from my eye, O companion, is pouring-down.
And the reproach — I bade-it-farewell on the day of the parting; and say: I remained alone, so no heart and no hope.
O my companion, stand with me until I bid-farewell to (her) from whose speech are-cured the sicknesses and the ailments.
sentences.i:
The parting has lasted long, and the care and the dread endure, and the tears, my friend, pour down from my eyes.
Even reproach I bade farewell on the day we parted — say it: I am left alone, with no heart and no hope.
Stand with me, my friend, until I say goodbye to her whose very speech cures every sickness and ill.
sentences.n: yā ṣāḥi is the clipped vocative of ṣāḥib, “companion”, common in verse; the print runs yā and ṣāḥi together (يَاصَاحِ), and one of its dots is faint in the scan, but only yā ṣāḥi gives sense. wa-qul, “and say”, is abrupt: the poet turns to his companion, or it stands loosely for wa-qultu, “and I said”. tashtafī, “find a cure”: the sicknesses themselves are healed by her words. The print writes tashtafī with a final ى. The rhyme is -lu throughout.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الشَّابَّ بَعْدَ مَا فَرَغَ مِنَ الشِّعْرِ بَكَى سَاعَةً وَغُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ وَتَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ نَاظِرٌ إِلَيْهِ وَهُوَ يَتَعَجَّبُ مِنْ أَمْرِهِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-shābba baʿda mā faragha mina al-shiʿri bakā sāʿatan wa-ghushiya ʿalayhi wa-tāju al-mulūki nāẓirun ilayhi wa-huwa yataʿajjabu min amrihi
sentences.l: Then the youth, after he finished from the poetry, wept an hour and was-fainted upon, and Tāj al-Mulūk (was) looking at him, and he was wondering at his affair.
sentences.i: When the young man had finished his poem he wept for a while and fainted, while Tāj al-Mulūk watched him, wondering what was the matter with him.
sentences.n: ghushiya ʿalayhi, literally “it was covered over him”, is the usual Arabic for fainting. sāʿatan, “an hour”, means “a while”.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ رَنَا بِفَاتِكِ اللَّحَظَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqa ranā bi-fātiki al-laḥaẓāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And when he came-to, he gazed with (eyes) killing of the glances, and recited these verses:
sentences.i: When he came to, he gazed out with glances that could kill, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: ranā, “to gaze steadily”. bi-fātiki al-laḥaẓāt, “with murderous glances”: bi-, “with”, and fātik, “slaying, reckless”, a stock phrase of love poetry for the lover’s or the beloved’s eyes.

sentences.t:
خُذُوا حِذْرَكُمْ مِنْ طَرْفِهَا فَهْوَ سَاحِرُ * وَلَيْسَ بِنَاجٍ مَنْ رَمَتْهُ الْمَحَاجِرُ
فَاِنَّ الْعُيُونَ السُّودَ وَهْيَ نَوَاعِسُ * تَقُدُّ السُّيُوفَ الْبِيضَ وَهْيَ بَوَاتِرُ
وَلَا تَخْدَعُوا مِنْ رِقَّةٍ فِي كَلَامِهَا * فَاِنَّ الْحُمَيَّا لِلْعُقُولِ تُخَامِرُ
مُنَعَّمَةُ الْاَطْرَافِ لَوْمَسَّ جِسْمَهَا * حَرِيرٌ لَادْمَاهُ وَهَا اَنْتَ نَاظِرُ
بَعِيدَةُ مَا بَيْنَ الْمُخَلْخَلِ وَالطُّلَا * وَاَيْنَ الشَّذَا مِنْ طِيبِهَا وَهْوَ عَاطِرُ
sentences.tr:
khudhū ḥidhrakum min ṭarfihā fa-hwa sāḥiru * wa-laysa bi-nājin man ramathu al-maḥājiru
fa-inna al-ʿuyūna al-sūda wa-hya nawāʿisu * taquddu al-suyūfa al-bīḍa wa-hya bawātiru
wa-lā takhdaʿū min riqqatin fī kalāmihā * fa-inna al-ḥumayyā li-al-ʿuqūli tukhāmiru
munaʿʿamatu al-aṭrāfi law massa jismahā * ḥarīrun la-admāhu wa-hā anta nāẓiru
baʿīdatu mā bayna al-mukhalkhali wa-al-ṭulā * wa-ayna al-shadhā min ṭībihā wa-hwa ʿāṭiru
sentences.l:
Take your caution from her glance, for it is a sorcerer; and not escaping is he whom the eye-sockets have shot.
For the eyes, the black ones — and they drowsy — cut the swords, the white ones, and they sharp-cutting.
And do not deceive from softness in her speech, for the strong-wine to the minds goes-to-the-head.
Soft-tended of the extremities: if there touched her body silk, it would have made-it-bleed — and here you are, looking.
Far is what (lies) between the anklet-place and the neck; and where is the fragrance from her scent, and it fragrant?
sentences.i:
Beware of her glance, for it is a sorcerer, and no one escapes whom those eyes have shot.
For black eyes, drowsy as they are, will cut through white swords, however keen.
Do not be beguiled by the softness of her speech, for strong wine goes to the head.
So delicately nurtured is she that silk, if it touched her body, would draw blood — and here you are, seeing it.
Long is the way from her anklets to her neck; and what is perfume beside her scent, fragrant though it is?
sentences.n: bi-nājin: bi- marks the predicate of laysa, “not (being) one who escapes”. al-maḥājir, “the eye-sockets”, stands for the eyes. al-ḥumayyā is wine at its sharpest; li-al-ʿuqūli tukhāmiru, “it gets into the minds”, the li- marking what it goes to. The print points takhdaʿū as active, “do not deceive”; the sense wants the passive, tukhdaʿū, “do not be deceived”, and it is translated so. baʿīdatu mā bayna al-mukhalkhali wa-al-ṭulā, “far between the anklet and the neck”, is a stock way of saying she is tall. The print runs law massa together (لَوْمَسَّ). The rhyme is -ru throughout.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ شَهَقَ شَهْقَةً فَغُشِيَ عَلَيْهِ فَلَمَّا رَأٰهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ عَلَى هَذِهِ الْحَالَةِ تَحَيَّرَ فِي أَمْرِهِ وَتَمَشَّى إِلَيْهِ
sentences.tr: thumma shahaqa shahqatan fa-ghushiya ʿalayhi fa-lammā raʾāhu tāju al-mulūki ʿalā hādhihi al-ḥālati taḥayyara fī amrihi wa-tamashshā ilayhi
sentences.l: Then he gasped a gasp and was-fainted upon; and when Tāj al-Mulūk saw him in this state, he was-perplexed in his affair and walked to him.
sentences.i: Then he gave a great gasp and fainted. When Tāj al-Mulūk saw him in this state he did not know what to make of him, and walked over to him.
sentences.n: The print spells raʾāhu, “he saw him”, without its long alif (رأه for رآه); it is pointed here with a dagger alif.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا أَفَاقَ مِنْ غَشْيَتِهِ نَظَرَ ابْنَ الْمَلِكِ وَاقِفًا عَلَى رَأْسِهِ فَنَهَضَ قَائِمًا عَلَى قَدَمَيْهِ وَقَبَّلَ الْأَرْضَ بَيْنَ يَدَيْهِ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā afāqa min ghashyatihi naẓara ibna al-maliki wāqifan ʿalā raʾsihi fa-nahaḍa qāʾiman ʿalā qadamayhi wa-qabbala al-arḍa bayna yadayhi
sentences.l: And when he came-to from his faint, he saw the son of the king standing over his head; so he rose standing on his two feet and kissed the ground between his two hands.
sentences.i: When he came out of his faint he saw the king’s son standing over him; he sprang to his feet and kissed the ground before him.
sentences.n: naẓara here takes a direct object, “he saw (him)”, without the usual ilā. bayna yadayhi, “between his hands”, means “before him”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ لِأَيِّ شَيْءٍ لَمْ تَعْرِضْ بِضَاعَتَكَ عَلَيْنَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu tāju al-mulūki li-ayyi shayʾin lam taʿriḍ biḍāʿataka ʿalaynā
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to him: For what thing did you not display your merchandise to us?
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said to him, “Why did you not show us your goods?”
sentences.n: li-ayyi shayʾin, “for what thing”: li-, “for”, asking the reason, “why”.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا مَوْلَايَ إِنَّ بِضَاعَتِي لَيْسَ فِيهَا شَيْءٌ يَصْلُحُ لِحَضْرَةِ سَعَادَتِكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā mawlāya inna biḍāʿatī laysa fīhā shayʾun yaṣluḥu li-ḥaḍrati saʿādatika
sentences.l: And he said: O my lord, my merchandise — there is not in it a thing (that) is-fit for the presence of your felicity.
sentences.i: He said, “My lord, there is nothing among my goods fit for Your Felicity.”
sentences.n: ḥaḍrat saʿādatika, “the presence of your felicity”, is a courtly form of address, like “Your Highness”; li-, “for”: fit for it.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَا بُدَّ أَنْ تَعْرِضَ عَلَيَّ مَا مَعَكَ وَتُخْبِرَنِي بِحَالِكَ فَإِنِّي أَرَاكَ بَاكِى الْعَيْنِ حَزِينَ الْقَلْبِ فَإِنْ كُنْتَ مَظْلُومًا أَزَلْنَا ظُلَامَتَكَ وَإِنْ كُنْتَ مَدْيُونًا قَضَيْنَا دَيْنَكَ فَإِنَّ قَلْبِي قَدِ احْتَرَقَ مِنْ أَجْلِكَ حِينَ رَأَيْتُكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lā budda an taʿriḍa ʿalayya mā maʿaka wa-tukhbiranī bi-ḥālika fa-innī arāka bākī al-ʿayni ḥazīna al-qalbi fa-in kunta maẓlūman azalnā ẓulāmataka wa-in kunta madyūnan qaḍaynā daynaka fa-inna qalbī qadi iḥtaraqa min ajlika ḥīna raʾaytuka
sentences.l: And he said: There is no escape (but) that you display to me what is with you and inform me of your state; for I see you weeping of the eye, sad of the heart. So if you are wronged, we remove your grievance; and if you are indebted, we pay your debt; for my heart has burned for your sake when I saw you.
sentences.i: He said, “You must show me what you have and tell me how it is with you, for I see your eyes weeping and your heart full of sorrow. If you have been wronged, we will right the wrong done to you, and if you are in debt, we will pay what you owe; for my heart burned for you the moment I saw you.”
sentences.n: The print puts a damma on the first letter of ʿalayya, “to me” (عُليّ), a slip of the type: the word can only be ʿalayya, and it is pointed so here. bi-ḥālika: the verb akhbara, “inform”, takes its matter with bi-, “of”. bākī al-ʿayn is spelt with a final ى. ẓulāma is a wrong one has suffered, a grievance to be redressed.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ تَاجَ الْمُلُوكِ أَمَرَ بِنَصْبِ كُرْسِيَّيْنِ فَنَصَبُوا لَهُ كُرْسِيًّا مِنَ الْعَاجِ وَالآبَنُوسِ مُشَبَّكًا بِالذَّهَبِ وَالْحَرِيرِ وَبَسَطُوا لَهُ بِسَاطًا مِنَ الْحَرِيرِ فَجَلَسَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ عَلَى الْكُرْسِيِّ وَأَمَرَ الشَّابَّ أَنْ يَجْلِسَ عَلَى الْبِسَاطِ
sentences.tr: thumma inna tāja al-mulūki amara bi-naṣbi kursiyyayni fa-naṣabū lahu kursiyyan mina al-ʿāji wa-al-ābanūsi mushabbakan bi-al-dhahabi wa-al-ḥarīri wa-basaṭū lahu bisāṭan mina al-ḥarīri fa-jalasa tāju al-mulūki ʿalā al-kursiyyi wa-amara al-shābba an yajlisa ʿalā al-bisāṭi
sentences.l: Then Tāj al-Mulūk ordered the setting-up of two chairs; and they set up for him a chair of the ivory and the ebony, latticed with the gold and the silk, and spread for him a carpet of the silk; and Tāj al-Mulūk sat on the chair and ordered the youth that he sit on the carpet.
sentences.i: Then Tāj al-Mulūk ordered two seats to be set out. They set up for him a chair of ivory and ebony worked in a lattice of gold and silk, and spread a silk carpet for him; Tāj al-Mulūk sat on the chair and told the young man to sit on the carpet.
sentences.n: amara bi-: the verb “order” takes the thing ordered with bi-. He calls for two seats, but only one chair is set up; the young man is given the carpet below him, so the seating shows the difference in their rank. mushabbak, “latticed, worked in openwork”.

sentences.t: وَقَالَ لَهُ اعْرِضْ عَلَيَّ بِضَاعَتَكَ
sentences.tr: wa-qāla lahu iʿriḍ ʿalayya biḍāʿataka
sentences.l: And he said to him: Display to me your merchandise.
sentences.i: He said to him, “Show me your goods.”
sentences.n: The print has بضاعنك, a misprint for بضاعتك, biḍāʿataka, “your goods”, corrected here.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ الشَّابُّ يَا مَوْلَايَ لَا تَذْكُرْ لِي ذَلِكَ فَإِنَّ بِضَاعَتِي لَيْسَتْ بِمُنَاسِبَةٍ لَكَ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu al-shābbu yā mawlāya lā tadhkur lī dhālika fa-inna biḍāʿatī laysat bi-munāsibatin laka
sentences.l: And the youth said to him: O my lord, do not mention to me that; for my merchandise is not suitable for you.
sentences.i: The young man said to him, “My lord, do not ask that of me, for my goods are not fit for you.”
sentences.n: laysat bi-munāsibatin: bi- marks the predicate after laysa, as often.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ لَا بُدَّ مِنْ ذَلِكَ ثُمَّ أَمَرَ بَعْضَ غِلْمَانِهِ بِإِحْضَارِهَا فَأَحْضَرُوهَا قَهْرًاعَنْهُ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu tāju al-mulūki lā budda min dhālika thumma amara baʿḍa ghilmānihi bi-iḥḍārihā fa-aḥḍarūhā qahran ʿanhu
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk said to him: There is no escape from that. Then he ordered some of his pages to bring it, and they brought it by-force against him.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk said, “It must be done.” Then he ordered some of his pages to fetch the goods, and they brought them in against the young man’s will.
sentences.n: qahran ʿanhu, “by force, in spite of him”; the print runs the two words together (قهراعنه). amara … bi-iḥḍārihā: bi- again carries the thing ordered.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا رَآهَا الشَّابُّ جَرَتْ دُمُوعُهُ وَبَكَى وَأَنَّ وَاشْتَكَى وَصَعَّدَ الزَّفَرَاتِ وَأَنْشَدَ هَذِهِ الْأَبْيَاتَ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā raʾāhā al-shābbu jarat dumūʿuhu wa-bakā wa-anna wa-ishtakā wa-ṣaʿʿada al-zafarāti wa-anshada hādhihi al-abyāta
sentences.l: And when the youth saw it, his tears ran, and he wept and moaned and complained, and sent-up the sighs, and recited these verses:
sentences.i: When the young man saw them his tears ran; he wept and moaned and lamented, heaved deep sighs, and recited these verses:
sentences.n: anna, “he moaned” (the print marks its shadda); ishtakā, “he complained”, chimes with bakā.

sentences.t:
بِمَا بِجَفْنِكَ مِنْ غُنْجٍ وَمِنْ كَحَلٍ * وَمَا بِقَدِّكَ مِنْ لِينٍ وَمِنْ مَيَلٍ
وَمَا بِثَغْرِكَ مِنْ خَمْرٍ وَمِنْ شَهْدِ * وَمَا بِطَبْعِكَ مِنْ لُطْفٍ وَمِنْ مَلَلِ
عِنْدِي زِيَارَةُ طَيْفٍ مِنْكَ يَا اَمَلِي * اَحْلَى مِنَ الْاَمْنِ عِنْدَ الْخَائِفِ الْوَجِلِ
sentences.tr:
bi-mā bi-jafnika min ghunjin wa-min kaḥalin * wa-mā bi-qaddika min līnin wa-min mayalin
wa-mā bi-thaghrika min khamrin wa-min shahdi * wa-mā bi-ṭabʿika min luṭfin wa-min malali
ʿindī ziyāratu ṭayfin minka yā amalī * aḥlā mina al-amni ʿinda al-khāʾifi al-wajili
sentences.l:
By what is in your eyelid of coquetry and of kohl-darkness, and what is in your stature of suppleness and of swaying,
And what is in your mouth of wine and of honey, and what is in your nature of gentleness and of weariness —
To me a visit of a phantom from you, O my hope, (is) sweeter than the safety to the fearful, the frightened.
sentences.i:
By the languor and the dark of your eyelids, by the suppleness and sway of your form,
By the wine and the honey of your lips, by the gentleness and the fickleness of your nature:
To me, my hope, a visit from your phantom is sweeter than safety to a frightened man.
sentences.n: bi-mā, “by what”: the bi- of oaths, and the oath runs through two lines before the poet says what he swears. In bi-jafnika, bi-qaddika and the rest, bi- means “in”. kaḥal is the natural darkness of the eyelids, as if lined with kohl. malal, “weariness, boredom”, is the beloved’s quickness to tire of a lover. ṭayf is the beloved’s image that visits in sleep. The print points shahdi without its tanwīn, where min shahdin is expected. The rhyme is -li throughout.

sentences.t: ثُمَّ إِنَّ الشَّابَّ فَتَحَ بِضَاعَتَهُ وَعَرَضَهَا عَلَى تَاجِ الْمُلُوكِ قِطْعَةً قِطْعَةً وَتَفْصِيلَةً تَفْصِيلَةً وَأَخْرَجَ مِنْ جُمْلَتِهَا ثَوْبًا مِنَ الْأَطْلَسِ مَنْسُوجًا بِالذَّهَبِ يُسَاوِي أَلْفَيْ دِينَارٍ
sentences.tr: thumma inna al-shābba fataḥa biḍāʿatahu wa-ʿaraḍahā ʿalā tāji al-mulūki qiṭʿatan qiṭʿatan wa-tafṣīlatan tafṣīlatan wa-akhraja min jumlatihā thawban mina al-aṭlasi mansūjan bi-al-dhahabi yusāwī alfay dīnārin
sentences.l: Then the youth opened his merchandise and displayed it to Tāj al-Mulūk piece by piece and length by length, and brought-out from its whole a robe of the satin woven with the gold, (that) was-worth two-thousand dinars.
sentences.i: Then the young man unpacked his goods and showed them to Tāj al-Mulūk piece by piece and length by length, and from among them he brought out a robe of satin woven with gold, worth two thousand dinars.
sentences.n: tafṣīla is a length of cloth cut for a garment. bi-al-dhahab, “with gold”: the bi- of the material.

sentences.t: فَلَمَّا فَتَحَ الثَّوْبَ وَقَعَتْ مِنْ وَسَطِهِ خِرْقَةٌ فَأَخَذَهَا الشَّابُّ بِسُرْعَةٍ وَوَضَعَهَا تَحْتَ وَرِكِهِ وَقَدْ ذَهَلَ عَنِ الْمَعْقُولِ وَأَنْشَدَ يَقُولُ
sentences.tr: fa-lammā fataḥa al-thawba waqaʿat min wasaṭihi khirqatun fa-akhadhahā al-shābbu bi-surʿatin wa-waḍaʿahā taḥta warikihi wa-qad dhahala ʿani al-maʿqūli wa-anshada yaqūlu
sentences.l: And when he opened the robe, there fell from its middle a rag; and the youth took it with speed and put it under his thigh, and he had become-distracted from the reasonable, and recited, saying:
sentences.i: When he unfolded the robe a scrap of cloth fell out of it. The young man snatched it up and put it under his thigh, quite beside himself, and recited:
sentences.n: khirqa, “a rag, a scrap of cloth”: its secret is what the tale now turns on. dhahala ʿani al-maʿqūl, “he was distracted from what is reasonable”: he lost his wits for a moment. bi-surʿatin, “with speed”, quickly.

sentences.t:
مَتَى يَشْتَفِي مِنْكَ الْفُوَادُ الْمُعَذَّبُ * وَنَجْمُ الثُّرَيَّا مِنْ وِصَالِكَ اَقْرَبُ
بِعَادٌ وَهَجْرٌ وَاشْتِيَاقٌ وَلَوْعَةٌ * وَمَطْلٌ وَتَسْوِيفٌ بِهِ الْعُمْرُ يَذْهَبُ
فَلَا الْوَصْلُ يُحْيِينِي وَلَا الْهَجْرُ قَاتِلِي * وَلَا الْبُعْدُ يُدْنِينِي وَلَا اَنْتَ تَقْرُبُ
وَمَا مِنْكَ اِنْصَافٌ وَلَا لَكَ رَحْمَةٌ * وَلَا مِنْكَ اِسْعَافٌ وَلَا عَنْكَ مَهْرَبُ
وَبِي حُبِّكُمْ ضَاقَتْ جَمِيعُ مَذَاهِبِي * عَلَيَّ فَلَا اَدْرِي اِلَى اَيْنَ اَذْهَبُ
sentences.tr:
matā yashtafī minka al-fuwādu al-muʿadhdhabu * wa-najmu al-thurayyā min wiṣālika aqrabu
biʿādun wa-hajrun wa-ishtiyāqun wa-lawʿatun * wa-maṭlun wa-taswīfun bihi al-ʿumru yadhhabu
fa-lā al-waṣlu yuḥyīnī wa-lā al-hajru qātilī * wa-lā al-buʿdu yudnīnī wa-lā anta taqrubu
wa-mā minka inṣāfun wa-lā laka raḥmatun * wa-lā minka isʿāfun wa-lā ʿanka mahrabu
wa-bī ḥubbikum ḍāqat jamīʿu madhāhibī * ʿalayya fa-lā adrī ilā ayna adhhabu
sentences.l:
When will be-cured by you the heart, the tormented, when the star of the Pleiades is nearer than union-with-you?
Distance and desertion and yearning and burning-pain, and putting-off and delaying, by which the life goes.
So neither the union revives me, nor the desertion (is) my killer; nor the distance brings-me-near, nor you come-near.
And there is not from you fairness, nor to you mercy; nor from you help, nor from you an escape.
And in me — (through) love of you there have become-narrow all my ways upon me, so I do not know to where I go.
sentences.i:
When will my tormented heart find its cure in you, when the Pleiades are nearer than union with you?
Distance, desertion, longing and the burning pain, delay and putting off — and so my life goes by.
Union does not revive me, desertion does not kill me; distance does not bring me near, nor do you come near.
You give no fairness and you show no mercy, you grant no help, and there is no escape from you.
For love of you all my ways have closed in on me, and I do not know where to go.
sentences.n: The print spells al-fuʾād, “the heart”, with a plain wāw, al-fuwād. The Pleiades are the proverbially distant stars. maṭl and taswīf are both the putting-off of a promise, “I’ll pay tomorrow”. wa-bī ḥubbikum in the last line is hard to construe as printed: “and in me, your love …”; it may stand for wa-fī ḥubbikum or wa-bi-ḥubbikum, “and through love of you”, and is translated in that sense, kept as printed. The poem shifts from “you” (singular) to “you” (plural) of the beloved, a common courtesy in verse. The rhyme is -bu throughout.

sentences.t: فَتَعَجَّبَ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ مِنْ إِنْشَادِهِ غَايَةَ الْعَجَبِ وَلَمْ يَعْلَمْ لِذَلِكَ مِنْ سَبَبٍ
sentences.tr: fa-taʿajjaba tāju al-mulūki min inshādihi ghāyata al-ʿajabi wa-lam yaʿlam li-dhālika min sababin
sentences.l: And Tāj al-Mulūk wondered at his reciting the utmost of the wonder, and did not know for that any cause.
sentences.i: Tāj al-Mulūk was utterly astonished at his verses and could not tell what lay behind them.
sentences.n: ghāyata al-ʿajab, “the utmost of wonder”, is an accusative of degree. li-dhālika min sababin, “for that any cause”: li-, “for”, and min marks “any” after the negative.

sentences.t: وَلَمَّا أَخَذَ الْخِرْقَةَ وَوَضَعَهَا تَحْتَ وَرِكِهِ قَالَ لَهُ تَاجُ الْمُلُوكِ مَا هَذِهِ الْخِرْقَةُ
sentences.tr: wa-lammā akhadha al-khirqata wa-waḍaʿahā taḥta warikihi qāla lahu tāju al-mulūki mā hādhihi al-khirqatu
sentences.l: And when he took the rag and put it under his thigh, Tāj al-Mulūk said to him: What (is) this rag?
sentences.i: When he had taken up the scrap and put it under his thigh, Tāj al-Mulūk said to him, “What is that piece of cloth?”

sentences.t: فَقَالَ يَا مَوْلَايَ لَيْسَ لَكَ بِهَذِهِ الْخِرْقَةِ حَاجَةٌ
sentences.tr: fa-qāla yā mawlāya laysa laka bi-hādhihi al-khirqati ḥājatun
sentences.l: And he said: O my lord, there is not to you with this rag a need.
sentences.i: He said, “My lord, you have no need of this scrap.”
sentences.n: ḥāja bi-, “need of”: the noun takes its object with bi-.

sentences.t: فَقَالَ لَهُ ابْنُ الْمَلِكِ أَرِنِي إِيَّاهَا
sentences.tr: fa-qāla lahu ibnu al-maliki arinī iyyāhā
sentences.l: And the son of the king said to him: Show-me it.
sentences.i: The king’s son said to him, “Show it to me.”
sentences.n: arinī iyyāhā: the verb “show” takes two objects; the second, “it”, stands apart on iyyā-.

sentences.t: قَالَ لَهُ يَا مَوْلَايَ أَنَا مَا امْتَنَعْتُ مِنْ عَرْضِ بِضَاعَتِي عَلَيْكَ إِلَّا لِأَجْلِهَا فَإِنِّي لَا أَقْدِرُ أَدَعُكَ تَنْظُرُ إِلَيْهَا
sentences.tr: qāla lahu yā mawlāya anā mā imtanaʿtu min ʿarḍi biḍāʿatī ʿalayka illā li-ajlihā fa-innī lā aqdiru adaʿuka tanẓuru ilayhā
sentences.l: He said to him: O my lord, I — I did not refuse from displaying my merchandise to you except for its sake; for I am not able (that) I let you look at it.
sentences.i: He said to him, “My lord, it was only because of this that I would not show you my goods, for I cannot let you look at it.”
sentences.n: The print has استنعت, a misprint for امتنعت, imtanaʿtu, “I refused”, corrected here. lā aqdiru adaʿuka, “I cannot let you”, without the an that Classical Arabic puts before the second verb, a Middle Arabic habit. li-ajlihā, “for its sake”.

sentences.t: وَأَدْرَكَ شَهْرَ زَادَ الصَّبَاحُ فَسَكَتَتْ عَنِ الْكَلَامِ الْمُبَاحِ
sentences.tr: wa-adraka shahrazāda al-ṣabāḥu fa-sakatat ʿani al-kalāmi al-mubāḥi
sentences.l: And the morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent from the permitted speech.
sentences.i: Morning overtook Shahrazād, and she fell silent, leaving the permitted speech.
sentences.n: The print sets the name as two words here, شهر زاد.
